newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Fuel crunch hits Nigerian commuters hard.
newsitem.headline: Fuel crunch hits Nigerian commuters hard.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of commuters were stranded in Lagos, Nigeria's commercial hub of six million people, on Monday as a five-week fuel shortage in Africa's leading crude oil producer showed no sign of abating.
"Urgent and drastic measures will be taken to solve the crisis," the military government's number two, Lieutenant-General Oladipo Diya, told reporters in the capital Abuja.

He said the government realised the situation was bad and the issue would be discussed on Monday at a monthly meeting of the defence and security committee which groups senior officers to find a "lasting solution."
No specific measures have so far been announced to end the crisis and many fuel dealers said they expected it to continue for sometime.
Witnesses said thousands of commuters trekked in rain-soaked Lagos as no buses were available to convey to them to work.
"I had to walk from home," said journalist Paul Okolo.

The few vehicles that manage to obtain fuel from a thriving black market charge 300 percent above the normal fares. Many workers, especially those in government ministries, are unable to afford the high fares and have chosen to stay at home.
"What's the point in going to the office?" asked Patricia Jack, a secretary in the Finance Ministry. "How much am I paid that I should spend all on transport - just 4,500 naira ($53)?"
Many private-sector firms have been forced to scale down operations because of the crisis, sending some staff on leave.
Uzor Okeke, director-general of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), has warned of an imminent collapse of industries if the situation does not improve soon.
He called the crisis "a national shame in a year that the government is pursuing poverty alleviation and production capacity enhancement programmes".
Newspaper reports said 10,000 tonnes of fuel arrived in Lagos at the weekend from the Warri refinery in the midwest but added that this was only enough to last the city three days.
One opposition newspaper said there was a peaceful demonstration in the northern city of Kano on Monday over the fuel crisis but this could not be independently confirmed.
Another said students had given the government an ultimatum to end the fuel crisis within 48 hours or face a nationwide demonstration.
Nigeria produces two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and has four oil refineries but suffers recurrent fuel shortages. The current one is the worst so far.
The four refineries have a combined capacity of 445,000 barrels of crude oil daily but produce only a fraction of capacity due to deteriorating facilities.
Last year, the government cut the allocation to the refineries by 50,000 bpd to 250,000 bpd and state oil company officials say this is one of the reasons for the fuel shortage.

They have also bandied other contradictory explanations for the fuel crisis such as ageing refineries, non-compliance with refinery maintenance schedules and non-disbursement of budgeted funds for the refineries by the federal authorities.

With Africa's most populous nation of 104 million dependent on road transport, the crisis is translating into higher prices for food as traders bringing in farm produce from rural areas face transport difficulties.
"We go to the interior to buy food items but we can't find transport to bring them in," said Chika Nwosu, a Lagos grocer, adding harvests were already being lost to the crisis.
